newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-U.S. data propels Wall Street, Eurobourses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.S. data propels Wall Street, Eurobourses.

text.p: European bourses, nervous that the global bull market may be ending, were prodded into life along with Wall Street on Tuesday when benign U.S. inflation figures reduced the chances of an early hike in U.S. interest rates.
The Dow, which had lost nearly 200 points over the previous three sessions, opened higher and was soon up more than one percent.

The weaker-than-expected U.S. employment costs data, which sent U.S. Treasury bonds soaring, boosted London's blue chip FTSE 100 index. The FTSE shook off its torpor and strode out of the red in afternoon trade, rising nearly half a percent by 1530 GMT.
It was a similar story in Frankfurt, which put on more than one percent, and on the Paris bourse, where the blue chip CAC-40 index was up more than 1.5 percent, scoring a new trading high.

There was excitement too on currency markets, where the dollar moved through a new four-year high of 121 yen after earlier touching a 31-month high of 1.6565 marks -- levels well above late Monday European levels of 1.6413 marks and 119.43 yen.
Financial markets had been anxiously awaiting the Employment Cost Index, which showed a smaller rise than Wall Street economists had been expecting.

The index was seen as key to any decision by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on interest rates at its meeting next week, especially after Fed chairman Alan Greenspan warned of risks of wage-driven inflation in his testimony to the U.S. Senate Budget Committee last week.

"Today's U.S. Q4 employment cost index is one of the most important economic releases of the week, if not the year if it marks a possible turning point in Fed monetary policy," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in his daily outlook on Tuesday.

The U.S. Treasury bond rallied about a full percentage point immediately after the report was released, with the yield on the benchmark 30-year treasury bond falling to 6.85 percent from 6.94 percent late Monday.
Meanwhile, analysts said the dollar was also helped by reports that neither Germany nor Japan appeared very worried about the dollar's strength against their currencies.
The dollar also touched a 33-month high of 1.4370 Swiss francs. It had retreated to 1.4325 by 1500 GMT but was still well above Monday's late European level of 1.4240.
The Swiss franc was unsettled overnight by a media report that Swiss Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger had said he was "relieved" at the currency's recent decline.

The U.S. data and Wall Street's recovery came like a shot in the arm to European bourses, where investors had been fretting over the future direction of U.,S. markets with some fearing the Dow could be on the verge of a more substantial fall.

"The figure wasn't hugely better than expected but it has calmed nerves," a London trader said. "Some people were expecting a nasty figure and the one we got was inoffensive. A U.S. rate increase next week is now pretty unlikely."

In Frankfurt floor trading closed down before the U.S. data and Wall Street opened for business. But in post bourse electronic trading German shares took off, also boosted by the stronger dollar, which makes German exports more attractive.
In Paris French stocks climbed sharply to set a record in afternoon trading with the blue chip CAC-40 index pushing well past its previous trading peak 2,463.91 set on set on 23 January.
CURRENCIES AT 1545 GMT
The dollar was at 121.38 yen and 1.6545 marks compared with late Europe's Monday level of 119.43 yen and 1.6413 marks.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1545 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares was up 16.7 points at 4,228.7.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index was up 41.36 to 2,476.53.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed down 5.2 at 2,989.33. The IBIS DAX index was up 36.33 points at 3,028.88.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $353.70 compared with London's Monday close of $354.60. Silver was just under the $5.0 level.
